```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                     fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.25)
```

A model covariate can be a kernel-weighted mean, a surface texture, or a
categorical landscape metric. That definition must survive preparation,
fitting, prediction, plotting, and model comparison. This guide follows those
steps and identifies the inference methods that support each feature.

Start with `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` for the basic
workflow. The artificial landscape below demonstrates software behavior. Its
counts do not provide evidence of scale recovery, ecological effects, or
interval coverage. Optimization and posterior fitting examples are not run
during the vignette build.

## Choose features and a fitting method

`kernel_var()` estimates the distance scale of an environmental mean.
`surface_var()` describes variation in a continuous surface, while
`landscape_var()` describes categorical composition or configuration. An
unweighted metric uses a circular neighborhood with a hard boundary. Its radius
can be fixed or estimated. A weighted surface metric uses the selected kernel
and estimates its bandwidth instead.

| Feature | Native refit | Analytic likelihood backends | Bayesian scales |
|:--------|:-------------|:----------------------------|:----------------|
| Kernel mean | Gaussian, exponential, exponential-power, or fixed kernel | Supported smooth kernels under the chosen backend's contract | Gaussian or exponential |
| Weighted surface SQ | Gaussian, exponential, or exponential-power | Gaussian or exponential, including mixtures with means | Gaussian or exponential, alone or with means |
| Weighted SA, skewness, or kurtosis | Gaussian, exponential, or exponential-power | Not implemented | Not implemented |
| Estimated hard-radius surface or landscape metric | Supported, including mixtures with exponential-power means | Not implemented for the discontinuous radius | Not implemented |
| Fixed-radius metric | Prepared once and used as a native predictor | Ordinary numeric predictor with verified original preparation | Ordinary numeric predictor with verified original preparation |

The analytic rows include `profile_glm`, `joint_nb2`, `conditional_logit`, and
`joint_mixed`, subject to their response and formula restrictions.
Exponential-power means are supported by the profile GLM/NB2 machinery;
the conditional-logistic, joint mixed, and Bayesian adapters require Gaussian or exponential
kernels. Analytic and Bayesian kernel means require distance bins. Weighted SQ
also needs retained raw cells, matching source definitions, and explicit row IDs.

A fixed-radius metric has no estimated bandwidth. Keep its original prepared
numeric column in the native model frame or Bayesian `data`. Analytic and
Bayesian fits use it like any other numeric covariate, including in a Bayesian
scale formula. It retains the mean and sample SD from the original preparation;
the prior-median reference for optimized spatial predictors does not replace
that normalization. Undefined and constant metrics remain preparation errors.

For new points, provide fixed columns explicitly or use `include_fixed = TRUE`
with matching spatial inputs. Automatic preparation verifies the original
source, metric, radius, kernel, resolution, buffer extent (`max_D`), and row identities.
Use the original buffer extent even when the fixed radius itself is smaller;
a shorter buffer can omit cells needed by the metric. It does not learn
a new center or SD from the prediction batch. Bayesian prediction and simulation
share this option, including repeated observations linked by explicit site IDs.
Fixed radii do not add an AIC parameter, a bandwidth prior, or scale uncertainty.

SQ is the square root of the weighted centered variance, with the sum of
weights in the denominator. Constant support has SQ zero. Standardized higher
moments are undefined at zero spread. Weighting removes discrete changes in
neighborhood membership, but does not make every metric differentiable at every
parameter value. The derivative-based methods therefore retain explicit
feature restrictions.

For native exponential-power mixtures, a hard-radius predictor has no shape
parameter. Its reported shape and shape SE are `NA`, and model selection
excludes the ignored shape position. The starting parameter vector keeps its
existing full layout. A fixed-radius metric has neither an estimated radius nor
an estimated shape. If all features are fixed, fit the native regression
directly to the prepared columns rather than asking for scale optimization.

## Prepare means, weighted SQ, and a fixed metric together

These two small surfaces share a projected square grid. Multiple covariates
can come from the same source raster; their aliases identify the model columns.

```{r artificial-surfaces}
hab <- terra::rast(nrows = 24, ncols = 24, xmin = 0, xmax = 240,
                   ymin = 0, ymax = 240, crs = "EPSG:3857")
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(hab, seq_len(terra::ncell(hab)))
terra::values(hab) <- sin(xy[, 1] / 17) + cos(xy[, 2] / 23) + xy[, 1] / 150
names(hab) <- "habitat"
elev <- hab
terra::values(elev) <- 30 + xy[, 1] / 8 + sin(xy[, 2] / 11) *
  (1 + xy[, 1] / 30) + cos(xy[, 1] / 13 + xy[, 2] / 19)
names(elev) <- "elevation"
landscape <- c(hab, elev)
locations <- expand.grid(x = seq(45, 195, 30), y = seq(45, 195, 30))
points <- terra::vect(as.matrix(locations), crs = terra::crs(hab))

features <- msr_vars(
  mean = kernel_var("habitat"),
  rough = surface_var("elevation", "sq", weighted = TRUE),
  fixed = surface_var("elevation", "sa", radius = 25)
)
prepared <- kernel_prep(points, landscape, max_D = 40,
  sigma = c(19, 29), scale_vars = features, bin = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
head(prepared$kernel_dat)
```

**How to read the output.** `mean` and `rough` are different variables with
starting bandwidths of 19 and 29 map units. `fixed` uses a radius of 25.
Preparation centers each column and divides by its sample SD. It does not
estimate a regression or select a scale. Keep the prepared row names when
joining responses and nonspatial predictors.

A native refit can use all three columns. Here `season` is a nonspatial factor,
and the counts are deterministic artificial values used only to illustrate the
calls. Heavy fitting remains explicit:

```{r native-starting-model}
dat <- prepared$kernel_dat
dat$season <- factor(rep(c("spring", "fall"), length.out = nrow(dat)))
dat$y <- (seq_len(nrow(dat)) %% 5L) + as.integer(dat$rough > 0)
model <- glm(y ~ mean + rough + fixed + season, data = dat, family = poisson())
```

```{r fit-refit, eval=FALSE}
fit <- multiScale_optim(model, prepared, backend = "refit", verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit)
profile <- profile_sigma(fit, n_pts = 10)
plot(profile)
```

**How to read these outputs.** `scale_est` reports the selected bandwidths in
map units. The fixed metric contributes a regression coefficient but no fitted
scale. Check convergence, search-bound, precision, and likelihood-profile
diagnostics before interpreting the selected values. A finite estimate or a
drawn curve does not establish identification. Hard-radius profiles can be
stepped and have no smooth-curvature scale SE.

For year-specific maps, use `kernel_prep_by_group()` and retain the map
assignment for every row. Optimization uses pooled training normalization.
Bayesian fits instead retain their declared pooled prior-reference
normalization for every draw. Neither workflow standardizes each projected
year separately. See `vignette("year-specific-rasters", package = "multiScaleR")`.

## Compare smoothing engines and prepare a map

Both FFT and direct focal calculation support the declared mean, surface, and
landscape metric families. The following calls use the same prepared circular
footprint. They perform no fitting:

```{r compare-smoothing}
map_fft <- kernel_scale.raster(landscape, multiScaleR = prepared,
  match_buffer = TRUE, fft = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
map_focal <- kernel_scale.raster(landscape, multiScaleR = prepared,
  match_buffer = TRUE, fft = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
max(abs(terra::values(map_fft) - terra::values(map_focal)), na.rm = TRUE)
terra::plot(map_fft[["rough"]], main = "Weighted SQ in source elevation units")
```

**How to read the output and map.** The printed maximum is the numerical
difference between engines. SQ describes local variation in elevation, not
mean elevation. The map retains the source units because this call did not
request standardization. Available finite cells are renormalized at edges, and
central source `NA` cells remain masked. With `na.rm = FALSE`, incomplete
footprints return `NA`; `match_buffer = TRUE` requires `na.rm = TRUE`.

The default `pct_wt` window remains available. For fitted raster prediction,
`match_buffer = TRUE` matches the retained preparation footprint, including
partially intersecting cells with their ordinary full-cell weights. Binning,
rasterization, incomplete source coverage, and the difference between an
arbitrary sample point and a cell center remain separate approximations.

## Predict points, scenarios, and rasters

For new points, prepare matching source definitions, then supply both their
data rows and spatial inputs. Selected scales and training normalization are
reused. Explicit `join_by` keys support repeated scenarios at the same site.
Verified fixed-radius normalization is opt-in:

```{r point-and-map-prediction, eval=FALSE}
# These rows and buffers illustrate the interface at the original locations.
point_prediction <- predict(fit, dat, prepared, include_fixed = TRUE,
  se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional")
snapshot <- prepare_prediction(fit, dat, prepared, include_fixed = TRUE)
predict(snapshot)

# Factors need explicit fitted levels. Numeric site variables use their
# native units, and offset_values contains raw inputs to offset expressions.
map_inputs <- kernel_scale.raster(landscape, multiScaleR = fit,
  scale_center = TRUE, include_fixed = TRUE, match_buffer = TRUE,
  site_values = list(season = "spring"), verbose = FALSE)
response_map <- predict(fit, map_inputs, se.fit = TRUE,
  uncertainty = "conditional", raster_args = list(cores = 1))
terra::plot(response_map)
```

**How to read the predictions.** Point estimates and maps describe the
provider's expected response or selected native component. An SE map conditions
on the selected spatial scales and excludes observation noise. Analytic
GLM/NB2 maps use the same retained coefficient information as point predictions.
Other native providers supply their own conditional SEs, when available.
An unavailable native SE raises an error rather than becoming zero.

Categorical scenarios retain fitted levels. Checked raster prediction restores
logical columns to their fitted type and preserves a `projection_contract`
with the preparation controls. Supply compound offset inputs explicitly, for
example `offset_values = c(effort = 2, duration = 4)` for
`offset(log(effort * duration))`. A log offset defaults to raw value one, while
a direct offset defaults to zero. Unknown scenario names are errors.

Random-effect controls keep their native meaning. For glmmTMB or lme4,
`native_args = list(re.form = NA)` sets response random effects to zero.
For nlme, use `native_args = list(level = 0)`. These are reference predictions,
not averages over a random-effect distribution. Cox maps describe linear
predictors or relative risks. Conditional-logistic response probabilities
require complete point choice sets; a raster can instead show link or relative
risk scores. Unmarked components such as state or detection must be selected
explicitly for raster prediction and retain their native row-layout rules.

A snapshot binds fixed rows, controls, and numerical results. Prepare it again
after changing any of them. Raster preparation descriptors check retained
definitions and scaling; they do not verify the scientific provenance of map
contents. Recompute after editing layers or using file formats that discard R
attributes.

## Plot effects and compare models with the appropriate target

```{r effects-and-selection, eval=FALSE}
plot_marginal_effects(fit)
null_model <- glm(y ~ 1, data = dat, family = poisson())
aic_tab(list(spatial = fit, null = null_model), AICc = FALSE)
bic_tab(list(spatial = fit, null = null_model))
```

**How to read the plots and tables.** Numeric effect panels vary one predictor
while holding the others at their means. Factor panels use observed levels.
Frequentist bands condition on selected spatial scales. Mixed-model panels use
native response means at zero random effects, including the fitted
zero-inflation or truncated-family mean where applicable. AIC/BIC counts include
estimated scales and applicable shapes, alongside the native likelihood
parameters. Fixed radii and inapplicable hard-radius shapes do not add to K.

Comparison requires the same used observations and comparable likelihoods.
Recoverable responses, row IDs, weights, binomial trials, likelihood measures,
ML/REML settings, and Cox strata are checked. Missing native metadata still
requires user judgment. REML comparisons require a common fixed-effect design.
Bayesian fits are rejected by `aic_tab()` and `bic_tab()` because their posterior
target includes priors. Posterior predictive comparison needs a separate
workflow with its own target and diagnostics.

For Bayesian fits, `plot_marginal_effects(bayes_fit)` uses stored
response-coefficient draws at hypothetical predictor values under the fixed reference
normalization. Its bands are central credible intervals. It sets response
random effects to zero and does not reevaluate the landscape at every kernel
draw. For location-specific posterior expectations, use
`predict(bayes_fit, ..., kernel_inputs = new_preparation)`; use `simulate()`
when observation variation is needed. A selected-scale raster cannot replace
posterior integration over scales. Private unpenalized marginal-likelihood SQ
limiting routines remain gated pending their separate rank and boundary audits.

| Output | Spatial scales | Included uncertainty |
|:-------|:---------------|:---------------------|
| Native-refit point or raster SE | Selected values held fixed | Native coefficient uncertainty, where available |
| Analytic GLM/NB2 joint point interval | Estimated scales and shapes | Joint coefficient/kernel information, if all gates pass |
| Bayesian spatial expectation | Recomputed for retained joint draws | Posterior uncertainty under the declared group policies |
| Bayesian effect panel | Fixed hypothetical reference-normalized covariates | Stored marginal coefficient draws |
| Bayesian observation simulation | Recomputed for retained joint draws | Posterior uncertainty plus observation variation |

## Quick reference

```{r full-workflow, eval=FALSE}
# 1. Declare features and preserve point IDs during preparation and joins.
prepared <- kernel_prep(points, landscape, max_D = 40,
  scale_vars = features, sigma = c(19, 29), bin = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
dat <- data.frame(y = dat$y, season = dat$season, prepared$kernel_dat)

# 2. Fit an appropriate likelihood and inspect its original diagnostics.
model <- glm(y ~ mean + rough + fixed + season, dat, family = poisson())
fit <- multiScale_optim(model, prepared, backend = "refit", verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit)

# 3. Reuse training normalization for points and an explicit map scenario.
predict(fit, dat, prepared, include_fixed = TRUE)
map_inputs <- kernel_scale.raster(landscape, multiScaleR = fit,
  scale_center = TRUE, include_fixed = TRUE, match_buffer = TRUE,
  site_values = list(season = "spring"), verbose = FALSE)
response_map <- predict(fit, map_inputs)

# 4. Read effects as conditional curves and compare sampling likelihoods.
plot_marginal_effects(fit)
aic_tab(list(fit, glm(y ~ 1, dat, family = poisson())), AICc = FALSE)
```

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `msr_vars()` | Name source-specific means and metrics |
| `kernel_prep()` / `kernel_prep_by_group()` | Prepare matching spatial rows and retain normalization |
| `multiScale_optim()` / `multiScale_bayes()` | Fit a supported likelihood or posterior target |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Evaluate the same declared features on a raster grid |
| `predict()` / `prepare_prediction()` | Predict with explicit spatial and uncertainty contracts |
| `plot_marginal_effects()` | Display conditional or hypothetical reference-covariate effects |
| `aic_tab()` / `bic_tab()` | Compare appropriate sampling likelihoods |
